analysis.one_liner: Bans credit card universal default, caps late fees, and requires lenders to check borrowers' ability to pay.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by a single senator, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped credit card companies from raising a cardholder's interest rate because of trouble on some other debt — the practice called universal default. It would have barred card companies from changing card terms without the cardholder's written agreement, capped late fees at roughly the cost the company actually incurs, and required lenders to check that a borrower can afford payments before issuing a card or raising its limit. The bill went to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders, especially those carrying balances who could see their interest rate jump after a late payment on an unrelated bill or a drop in their credit score. The bill also would have helped new borrowers by requiring lenders to verify income and obligations before extending credit, and it would have protected cardholders from 'gotcha' late fees on payments postmarked by the stated deadline.

how_it_helps.text: Bars card issuers from using adverse information — such as anything on a credit report or a change in the consumer's credit score — as grounds for raising a card's interest rate or ending an introductory rate, with exceptions only for index-based rates and actions directly on that same account.

Prohibits card issuers from changing the terms of a card agreement without the consumer's specific written consent, and lets cardholders pay off existing balances under the terms in effect when they borrowed.

Caps late fees, over-limit fees, and penalty rate increases at an amount reasonably related to the card issuer's actual cost, and blocks late fees or penalty rates when a payment is postmarked or initiated electronically by the required date.

Requires card issuers to determine, before opening an account or raising a credit limit, that the consumer can make the scheduled payments based on income, existing obligations, and employment status.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and card companies — would give up revenue from universal default rate hikes, penalty fees, and unilateral contract changes, and would face a screening requirement that could limit how much credit they extend to higher-risk borrowers.

drawbacks.text: The ability-to-pay verification requirement would have made it harder for lower-income borrowers to get or expand credit, since lenders could no longer open accounts or raise limits without confirming the borrower can make scheduled payments.

Capping fees and penalty rates at the issuer's cost could push card companies to recover that revenue elsewhere, such as through higher interest rates or annual fees, and could lead them to extend less credit overall.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted practices that at the time could triple a cardholder's interest rate based on unrelated debts and generated large fee income from small mistakes. The tradeoff is real but modest: some borrowers with shaky finances would find credit harder to get or more expensive up front, in exchange for protections against penalty-rate escalation and unilateral term changes for everyone carrying a balance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Menendez introduced the Credit Card Reform Act of 2006 in the Senate on April 26, 2006.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day it was introduced, and the action record shows no further activity for the remainder of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: universal default rate increases, penalty fees, and unilateral changes to card agreements all remained lawful, and cardholders continued to bear those costs. Borrowers gained nothing because the bill never received committee or floor consideration.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor; no other senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the remainder of the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never registered on the record; the bill sat in a committee led by a Republican majority for the rest of the Congress.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and card companies)
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated two major profit sources: penalty interest rates triggered by unrelated credit problems (universal default) and late/over-limit fees not tied to the issuer's actual cost, while barring unilateral changes to card terms. Issuers' interest in keeping these practices ran directly against cardholders' interest in predictable rates and terms.

industries.industry: Consumer reporting agencies and credit score providers
industries.note: The bill would have reduced one use of credit data — triggering card rate hikes — but the data themselves would still be collected and used for underwriting and other lending decisions.
